assessmentSummary.identity: A no-sprint initiation-control drill: the athlete leans forward as one aligned body, recovers with a step before falling, catches in a stable split stance, and holds the terminal position.
currentCardFindings: The name says position hold, but the description includes a dynamic fall, recovery step, catch, and hold; the terminal action distinguishes it from sprinting falling starts.
The card does not specify lead-side alternation, lean threshold, hold duration, landing foot position, arm position, balance criteria, or exit.
Existing falling-start sprint videos are non-exact adjacent candidates and cannot be approved for the hold without full sequence review.

proposedDosage.progressWhen: both sides catch quietly at a repeatable threshold and hold without extra steps

athleteInstructions: Lean forward, recover with one step, stop in a stable split stance, and hold without sprinting away

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Retain as a distinct no-sprint fall-to-catch definition, not an alias of Falling Start 10m. Quarantine until the single-step catch, side alternation, hold criteria, and exact media are human-reviewed.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Athlete starts standing, falls forward with a straight body line until near loss of balance, then catches in a sprint-ready split stance with shin angles and arm position set. Hold or reset without sprinting away.

evidence.sourceTitle: The difference is in the start: impact of timing and start procedure on sprint running performance
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Start procedure and start position materially affect measured sprint performance, while metres, yards, and a finish marker describe dosage and logistics rather than a new movement identity.

Falling Start Position Hold must state whether the athlete falls and accelerates through a distance or catches the fall and holds without sprinting; generic speed, neural, approach, and cone wording does not create a separate exercise.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical Performance Factors in the Track and Field Sprint Start: A Systematic Review
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
claims: The start, push-off, and first acceleration steps are related but distinguishable phases of short sprint acceleration.

Falling Start Position Hold is either a standing falling-start short acceleration or a no-sprint fall-to-split-stance control task; measurement unit, finish cone, and a 5-to-10-yard range remain delivery data.

evidence.sourceTitle: Sprint Acceleration Mechanics: The Major Role of Hamstrings in Horizontal Force Production
claims: Sprint acceleration uses coordinated hip, knee, and ankle actions, with hamstring contribution to horizontally oriented force production.

The acceleration card should identify gluteal, hamstring, quadriceps, plantar-flexor, hip-flexor, foot, lumbopelvic, and arm-action roles; the catch-and-hold version shifts emphasis toward braking, single-leg stance control, and trunk stabilization.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical Performance Factors in the Track and Field Sprint Start: A Systematic Review
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
claims: Early acceleration performance is associated with forward-directed impulse, propulsive force, and progressive projection through the first steps.

The forward fall is an initiation constraint, not proof of an ideal universal body angle; require a controlled whole-body lean, a timely recovery step, continued acceleration through the target, and an anthropometrically appropriate setup.

evidence.sourceTitle: The difference is in the start: impact of timing and start procedure on sprint running performance
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Different start procedures create different timing and body-position effects and should not share one generic difficulty value.

Exercise difficulty must directly score technical complexity, physical and absolute-load demand, coordination, supervision, failure consequence, impact, work-capacity demand, and overall difficulty; athlete experience remains programming context.

evidence.sourceTitle: Correlations between muscle-tendon parameters and acceleration ability in 20 m sprints
claims: Power output is highest during the first steps of sprint acceleration, so a short distance does not make maximal starts negligible load.

Falling Start Position Hold needs distance, intent, timed or untimed status, total high-speed contacts, surface, footwear, posterior-chain and plantar-flexor stress, technical-fatigue markers, recovery, and session sprint-volume accounting.
Quality sprint work requires a suitable surface, marked start and finish, sufficient run-out, and recovery that preserves speed quality.
Require a clear level dry lane, safe separation, suitable footwear, a finish and run-out zone, and readiness to control the forward fall; a cone may mark distance but does not define the exercise.
Acceleration sessions should prescribe distance, intensity, repetitions, sets, and recovery rather than repetitions alone.

For high-intent falling starts, use 2-6 efforts over 5-20 metres with approximately 60-180 seconds recovery according to distance and athlete response; prescribe the catch-and-hold task by clean attempts and hold seconds, not sprint distance.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical Performance Factors in the Track and Field Sprint Start: A Systematic Review
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
claims: The setup should support rapid hip extension and forward propulsion without forcing an inappropriate first-step geometry.

Use a small cue set: stand as one line, let the lean develop without bending at the waist, recover before a stumble, push the ground backward, coordinate the arms, accelerate through the target, and use the full run-out.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Training should use qualified supervision, correct technique, manageable demands, and gradual progression.

Stop for pain, limping, repeated stumble, an early reaching step, waist break, head-first fall, unsafe surface or spacing, loss of projection or arm-leg coordination, marked speed decline, collision risk, or failure to decelerate in the run-out.
Acceleration and maximal-velocity sprinting are distinct qualities and quality sprint work should not be converted into dense conditioning.

Falling Start Position Hold belongs after preparation and before fatiguing work; use the catch-and-hold task as a lower-speed initiation and position constraint, not as an equivalent dose of maximal acceleration.
Acceleration develops across successive steps rather than by immediately standing upright.

Show the whole-body fall, recovery threshold, first three contacts, target and run-out, an early-step regression, and the difference between accelerating through the target and catching the fall into a stable hold.
Coaches should distinguish acceleration quality from maximal velocity and conditioning.

Provide side and rear observation, start consistency, step and distance counts, timing method when used, projection and force-direction notes, arm-leg coordination, symptom and speed-loss stops, and exact merge or alias guidance.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Training and Long-Term Athletic Development
claims: Speed work should be developmentally appropriate and based on movement competency.

Accessibility options include a smaller lean, fall-to-step without sprint, two-point start instead of falling start, shorter distance, submaximal intent, visual start and finish marks, extra demonstration, untimed attempts, and longer recovery.

evidence.sourceTitle: The difference is in the start: impact of timing and start procedure on sprint running performance
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Start position and timing procedure can change the task and measured result.

Five versus ten yards, ten yards versus ten metres, generic sprint wording, and a finish cone are dosage or logistics annotations; fall-to-hold, resisted starts, cue-response starts, and other starting positions require controlled variants or distinct definitions.
